Behavioural simply means "relating to behaviour."

And behaviour, in turn, means the way a person (or an animal, or even a group) acts — what they do, how they react, how they conduct themselves in different situations.

So whenever you see the word behavioural placed before a noun, it is telling you: "this thing has something to do with behaviour." It is a describing word (an adjective) that connects any noun it's attached to with the idea of behaviour.

That's the simple version.
What Exactly Does "Relating to Behaviour" Mean?

The phrase "relating to behaviour" can mean several things depending on the context:

  • Caused by behaviour — a behavioural problem means a problem that comes from the way someone acts.
  • Studied through behaviour — behavioural science means a field that studies people or animals by observing what they do.
  • Aimed at changing behaviour — behavioural therapy means a type of treatment that works by changing how someone acts.
  • Involving behaviour as a factor — behavioural economics means an area of economics that takes human behaviour into account.

In every case, the word is pointing you toward observable actions — things that can actually be seen, measured, or noticed — rather than, say, purely internal feelings or abstract thoughts.

1. In Psychology and Mental Health

This is probably the most common place you'll meet this word. Phrases like behavioural therapy or behavioural disorder are everywhere in mental health discussions.

  • A behavioural disorder is a condition where a person's pattern of actions is consistently disruptive, harmful, or socially unacceptable — such as extreme aggression or chronic lying.
  • Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is one of the most widely used forms of mental health treatment in the world. It focuses on identifying unhelpful patterns of thinking and acting, and then replacing them with healthier ones. The "behavioural" part means the therapy pays close attention to what the person does, not just what they feel or think.
  • A behavioural symptom is a sign of a condition that shows up in how someone acts — for example, a child with anxiety might show behavioural symptoms like refusing to go to school or throwing tantrums.

2. In Science and Research

Behavioural science is an umbrella term for all the fields of study that try to understand human (and animal) actions using systematic observation and research. This includes psychology, sociology, anthropology, and more.

A behavioural study is a piece of research that looks at what people or animals actually do under various conditions. When scientists talk about behavioural patterns, they mean recurring, consistent ways in which a subject acts over time — for example, the behavioural patterns of wolves when hunting, or the behavioural patterns of teenagers when using social media.

3. In Economics and Business

Behavioural economics is a field that blends psychology with economics. Traditional economics assumed people always make perfectly logical, rational decisions. Behavioural economics challenges this by showing that real human decision-making is shaped by emotions, biases, habits, and social pressures — in other words, by behaviour. A business might use behavioural data (information about what customers actually do — what they click, buy, or ignore) to design better products or services.

4. In Education

Teachers and school professionals often talk about behavioural issues or behavioural challenges to describe students who act in ways that interfere with learning or the classroom environment — things like constant disruption, defiance, or inability to sit still. A behavioural assessment in a school setting is an evaluation of how a child acts in order to understand their needs better.

5. In Everyday Life

You don't need to be a scientist to use this word. In everyday conversation, people say things like:

  • "The dog has some behavioural issues — it barks at strangers."
  • "The programme focuses on behavioural change."
  • "Her behavioural patterns shifted after the move."

In all these cases, the word is simply flagging that we are talking about actions and conduct, not opinions, feelings, or beliefs.

Here are the most important combinations to know, as they appear frequently in reading and conversation:

  • Behavioural pattern — a repeated, consistent way of acting over time.
  • Behavioural change — a shift in the way someone acts, often deliberately sought through therapy, education, or intervention.
  • Behavioural science — the study of how people and animals behave.
  • Behavioural therapy — a form of treatment that targets and modifies specific actions.
  • Behavioural disorder — a condition characterised by persistent, problematic patterns of action.
  • Behavioural traits — specific characteristics visible through the way someone acts (e.g., impulsiveness or shyness).
  • Behavioural economics — the study of economic decisions through the lens of real human behaviour.
  • Behavioural assessment — a formal evaluation of how someone acts, used to guide treatment or support.

Sometimes people contrast behavioural with emotional or cognitive:

  • Cognitive = relating to thinking and mental processes.
  • Emotional = relating to feelings.
  • Behavioural = relating to actions and conduct.

For example, a child struggling in school might have cognitive difficulties (trouble understanding the material), emotional difficulties (anxiety or sadness), or behavioural difficulties (acting out, refusing to work) — or a combination. Knowing which type of difficulty is involved points professionals toward the right kind of support.

This distinction shows you that behavioural has a specific territory: it lives in the world of what is done, not what is thought or felt — though of course, in real life, all three are deeply connected.

You will also see this word spelled "behavioral" — without the 'u'. Both mean exactly the same thing. Behavioural is the standard spelling in British, Australian, and most Commonwealth English. Behavioral is the American English spelling. Neither is wrong — they are simply regional variations of the same word.

Behavioural is an adjective that describes anything connected to, caused by, studied through, or aimed at changing the way a person or animal acts — it is the lens of "observable action" applied to whatever noun follows it.
